sections.b: Judith enters the book only in chapter 8: a widow of the tribe of Simeon, rich, beautiful and devout, who has fasted on her roof for more than three years (8:1–8). She rebukes the elders for setting God a deadline (8:11–27), prays for God to strike the enemy "by the deceit of my lips" (9:10), dresses for the enemy camp (10:3–4), deceives Holofernes with a speech full of double meanings (11:5–19), keeps the food laws in his tent (12:1–4), and beheads him with his own sword (13:6–8). She shows the head at Bethulia's gate (13:15), is blessed by Uzziah and by the high priest (13:18; 15:9–10), leads the women in a song like Miriam's (16:1–17), and lives as a widow to 105 (16:22–23). The book insists both on her deceit and on her chastity: "my face deceived him... but he did no sin with me" (13:16).

The Greek Judith never mentions Hanukkah, but its procession with thyrsi (Judith 15:12) uses the word of 2 Maccabees 10:7 for the first Hanukkah, and many scholars think it was written for readers who knew the Maccabean victory. In the Middle Ages the link became explicit: Hebrew retellings set the story in the Maccabean war and were read at Hanukkah, the Tosafot named Judith as the woman through whom the miracle came (on Megillah 4a), and the Rema recorded the custom of eating cheese because of the milk she fed the enemy (Orach Chayim 670:2). The Vulgate's claim that her victory became a Jewish holy day (Vulgate Judith 16:31) has no support in Jewish sources.

Judith fasts "every day of her widowhood" except Sabbaths, new moons and feasts and the days before them (Judith 8:6), a rule of life rather than a fast for one crisis, like the widow Anna's in the Temple (Luke 2:37). Her exceptions show that fasting gives way to the joy of holy days, as the Mishnah later forbade public fasts on new moons and festivals (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:10). The card at Judith 8 compares the churches' views on fixed fast days.

sections.h: Judith, the widow who saved Israel
sections.b: Judith is the great rich widow of Jewish tradition: she owns and runs her husband's estate (Judith 8:7), lives in prayer and fasting (Judith 8:5–6), calls on the God who hears widows (Judith 9:4, 9), and never remarries (Judith 16:22). Ambrose and Jerome held her up as a model of Christian widowhood. The card at Judith 16 compares the churches' views on whether lifelong widowhood or celibacy is a higher calling.

sections.h: Judith as a figure of Mary
sections.b: Uzziah blesses Judith "by God Most High above all the women on earth" (Judith 13:18), and the high priest calls her Jerusalem's honor and Israel's delight (Judith 15:9). The Latin church has long sung these words of Mary, above all on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, and read Judith's blow to the enemy's head with Genesis 3:15. Protestant churches do not use them so. The card at Judith 15 sets out the views.

Judith prays for God to break the Assyrians' pride (Judith 9:7–10), kills their general (Judith 13:8) and sends Israel out to rout the leaderless army (Judith 14:1–4; 15:1–7). As in Judges, God works by panic and through the weak (Judith 15:2; Judges 7:22), and the victors purify themselves and dedicate the spoil (Judith 16:18–19). The deep section on Judith 13 sets out how readers have judged the killing.

Judith is modeled on Jael and Deborah. Deborah promised that "the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hands" (Judges 4:9); Judith prays to break the enemy "by a woman's hand" (Judith 9:10). Jael killed the sleeping Sisera in her tent; Judith beheads the drunken Holofernes in his. Jael is "Blessed above women" (Judges 5:24); Judith is blessed "above all the women on earth" (Judith 13:18). Both stories end in a song (Judges 5; Judith 16).

sections.b: Achior, an Ammonite, "believed in God completely", was circumcised and "joined to the house of Israel, to this day" (Judith 14:10), though Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Ammonites from the assembly. The Mishnah allowed an Ammonite convert on the ground that Sennacherib had mixed the nations (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4).

Achior believes first and is circumcised after (Judith 14:10), the order Paul stresses for Abraham (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:9–12). For Judith circumcision is still how a believing Gentile joins Israel, as in the Hasmonean age, when John Hyrcanus required it of the Idumeans (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258).

Judith's song (Judith 16:1–17) is one of the last of the great victory songs led by women in Jewish tradition. It quotes the Greek of Exodus 15:3, "the Lord who shatters wars" (Judith 9:7; 16:2), recalls the enemy's boasts as in Exodus 15:9 (Judith 16:4), and is sung with dancing women and tambourines as Miriam's was (Exodus 15:20–21; Judith 15:12–16:1).

Judith prays for God to strike the enemy "by the deceit of my lips" (Judith 9:10) and deceives Holofernes at length (Judith 11:5–19). Readers have compared her with Rahab, the Hebrew midwives (Exodus 1:19–20) and Samuel's cover story (1 Samuel 16:2). Aquinas held that Judith was praised for her zeal to save the people, not for the lie (Summa II-II q.110 a.3 ad 3).

sections.b: Judith reads like a story for the generation after the Maccabees: zeal like Phinehas' and Mattathias' (Judith 9:4; 1 Maccabees 2:24–26), a threatened Temple, a high priest and council ruling from Jerusalem (Judith 15:8), an enemy general's head hung up as Nicanor's was (Judith 14:1; 1 Maccabees 7:47), and a procession with thyrsi like the one at the Temple's purification (Judith 15:12; 2 Maccabees 10:7).

sections.b: Judith opens her prayer by praising the God who put the sword in Simeon's hand to avenge Dinah (Judith 9:2–4). Genesis instead ends with Jacob's curse on that anger (Genesis 49:5–7), while Jubilees 30 and the Testament of Levi praise the brothers' zeal, as Judith does.

Christian readers saw in Judith a figure of Mary, of the church and of the soul defeating the devil, reading her blow to Holofernes' head with Genesis 3:15. Luther instead read the book as an allegory of the Jewish people (Judith, "Jewish woman") against the godless ruler.

Judith brings her own bread, wine, oil, grain and figs into the enemy camp and refuses Holofernes' food "so that it will not become a stumbling block" (Judith 10:5; 12:1–4, 19), like Daniel (Daniel 1:8) and Tobit (Tobit 1:10–11). In her false story, the starving town's sin is eating forbidden animals and the priests' portions (Judith 11:12–13).

After the victory the women of Israel dance for Judith, and she leads them, crowned with olive, as Miriam led the women with tambourines (Judith 15:12–13; Exodus 15:20–21). Her song begins with a call to tambourines (Judith 16:1).

Judith's song ends: the Lord Almighty "will put fire and worms into their flesh, and they will weep and feel it forever" (Judith 16:17). The line takes up Isaiah 66:24, where the worm and fire consume corpses, and goes beyond it to a punishment that the nations feel without end, one of the earliest Jewish statements of the idea.

Judith tells the elders that the siege is not punishment, since they have not worshiped idols, but testing, as God tested Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that "the Lord whips those who come near him, to warn them" (Judith 8:18–27). The right response is thanks, not deadlines.

After the killing, Judith sends for Achior so that he can see the head of the man who sent him to Bethulia to die (Judith 14:5). He faints, then falls at her feet and blesses her "in every tent of Judah" (Judith 14:6–7). Hearing her story, "he believed in God completely", was circumcised, and "was joined to the house of Israel, to this day" (Judith 14:10). Faith comes first and circumcision follows, the order Paul stresses for Abraham (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:9–12). Judith had earlier used Achior's creed, that Israel falls only when it sins, as the bait for her trap (Judith 11:9–11).

Judith flatters Holofernes by swearing "as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, lives", and borrows Jeremiah's and Daniel's language that even the wild animals serve the king (Judith 11:7; Jeremiah 27:6; Daniel 2:38). The book's answer to his claim to be god (Judith 6:2) comes in Bagoas' cry over the headless general: "One Hebrew woman has brought shame on the house of King Nebuchadnezzar!" (Judith 14:18). The Persian names of Holofernes and Bagoas and the "Persians and Medes" of Judith 16:10 suggest that the book's Nebuchadnezzar is a composite tyrant.
